language model (LLM)-powered retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems significantly reduce factual errors in question answering, but they present a novel and under-investigated attack surface: factual information in retrieved text can be exposed in ways that do not align with the disclosure norms of the information itself. In legal, medical, and enterprise environments, this leakage is not only a confidentiality violation but a contextual integrity (CI) violation, where privacy is understood as the appropriate flow of information between roles and for specific purposes. Current defenses are mostly input minimizers or post hoc output filters that are blind to the circumstances of the data source (sender, recipient, purpose), creating a structural gap between the document store and the model generation step. We introduce ContextGuard-RAG, a multi-agent privacy enforcement framework that embeds CI theory directly into the retrieval and generation pipeline. It consists of three tightly coupled components: a CI-policy encoder that attaches sender, recipient, subject, information-type, and transmission-principle norms to retrieved contexts from document metadata; a privacy-aware reranker that filters contexts violating inferred CI norms using a fine-tuned cross-encoder classifier; and a generative firewall agent that sanitizes output using reinforcement learning to avoid transitive leakage through document-derived hallucinations or indirect inferences. On PrivacyQA, MedQA, and LegalBench, ContextGuard-RAG reduces CI violations by about 34 percent relative to vanilla RAG, by 13.5 percent on average over AirGapAgent, and by 10 percent on average over the 1-2-3 Check multi-agent reasoning approach, while achieving parity with the best accuracy baseline in ROUGE-L (within 0.6 absolute points) and remaining stable under context-hijacking adversarial probes. Unlike prior approaches, ContextGuard-RAG performs norm-aware retrieval rather than post hoc filtering and benefits four backbone LLMs without retraining the upstream Generation (RAG) enables language models to generate responses using information retrieved from external knowledge sources. Although retrieval can improve grounding, it also introduces privacy risks when the underlying knowledge base contains sensitive information. A RAG system may retrieve documents containing personally identifiable information and subsequently reproduce that information in generated responses. This study evaluates sensitive-information leakage and redaction-based privacy protection in a controlled biomedical RAG environment.\n<div>\n A privacy benchmark was constructed using the 1,000-example labeled subset of PubMedQA by augmenting a fixed subset of 178 documents with synthetic patient records containing fictitious names, phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security number-like identifiers, and medical record numbers. No real patient information was used. A total of 890 targeted extraction attacks were generated to evaluate whether a RAG pipeline could disclose these synthetic identifiers. The baseline system used Sentence-BERT embeddings, FAISS dense retrieval, and FLAN T5-base for answer generation.\n<\/div>\n<div>\n Under the initial controlled privacy benchmark, the standard RAG configuration disclosed the exact synthetic secret in 60.11% of extraction attacks. The target document was retrieved at rank 1 in 98.20% of attacks, and leakage among attacks with correct rank-1 retrieval was 61.21%. Deterministic redaction designed for the known synthetic identifier formats reduced exact-secret leakage to 0.00% while preserving retrieval and question-answering utility on the 178 modified documents.\n<\/div>\n<div>\n A second robustness experiment evaluated 250 balanced extraction attacks after sensitive identifiers were transformed into alternative formatting variants not recognized by the original format-specific redactor. Under this format shift, standard RAG and the original format-specific redaction both produced a 63.20% exact-secret leakage rate. In contrast, a broader rule-based privacy-aware redaction mechanism reduced measured exact-secret leakage to 0.00%. Retrieval performance remained effectively unchanged: Recall@5 was 99.44% and MRR was 99.16% for both basic and privacy-aware redaction in the final utility evaluation. Answer accuracy changed from 41.57% to 42.70%.&nbsp;\n<\/div>\n<div>\n These results demonstrate, within the controlled synthetic benchmark, that format-specific redaction can be brittle under representation changes even when it performs perfectly on known formats. Broader privacy-aware redaction substantially reduced exact disclosure without measurable retrieval degradation in the evaluated setting. The findings provide an empirical framework for studying privacy\u2013utility tradeoffs in retrieval-augmented biomedical question answering. Sciences"],"abstract":"<jats:p>In this paper, we describe our biomedical document retrieval system and answers extraction module, which is part of the biomedical question answering system. Approximately 26.5 million PubMed articles are indexed as a corpus with the Apache Lucene text search engine. Our proposed system consists of three parts. The first part is the question analysis module, which analyzes the question and enriches it with biomedical concepts related to its wording. The second part of the system is the document retrieval module. In this step, the proposed system is tested using different information retrieval models, like the Vector Space Model, Okapi BM25, and Query Likelihood. The third part is the document re-ranking module, which is responsible for re-arranging the documents retrieved in the previous step. For this study, we tested our proposed system with 6B training questions from the BioASQ challenge task. We obtained the best MAP score on the document retrieval phase when we used Query Likelihood with the Dirichlet Smoothing model. We used the sequential dependence model at the re-rank phase, but this model produced a worse MAP score than the previous phase. In similarity calculation, we included the Named Entity Recognition (NER), UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers (CUI), and UMLS Semantic Types of the words in the question to find the sentences containing the answer. Using this approach, we observed a performance enhancement of roughly 25% for the top 20 outcomes, surpassing another method employed in this study, which relies solely on textual similarity.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.3390\/app14062613","type":"journal-article","created":{"date-parts":[[2024,3,20]],"date-time":"2024-03-20T13:09:36Z","timestamp":1710940176000},"page":"2613","update-policy":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.3390\/mdpi_crossmark_policy","source":"Crossref","is-referenced-by-count":4,"title":["Document Retrieval System for Biomedical Question Answering"],"prefix":"10.3390","volume":"14","author":[{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0000-0003-3119-404X","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Harun","family":"Bolat","sequence":"first","affiliation":[{"name":"Computer Engineering Department, Ankara Y\u0131ld\u0131r\u0131m Beyaz\u0131t University, 06010 Ankara, Turkey"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0000-0003-3577-2548","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Baha","family":"\u015een","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[{"name":"Computer Engineering Department, Ankara Y\u0131ld\u0131r\u0131m Beyaz\u0131t University, 06010 Ankara, Turkey"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"member":"1968","published-online":{"date-parts":[[2024,3,20]]},"reference":[{"key":"ref_1","doi-asserted-by":"crossref","first-page":"1","DOI":"10.1016\/j.cmpb.2009.10.003","article-title":"Biomedical question answering: A survey","volume":"99","author":"Athenikos","year":"2010","journal-title":"Comput.
